articles.title: Apple launches new Health AI study app to understand how people use AI for medical advice
articles.summary: Apple has launched the new Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States.
articles.body: Apple has launched the new Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States. It is a virtual research study and associated app which is designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”Dedicated app allows users to ask health questionsAs part of the initiative, Apple has released a dedicated iOS app that lets participants ask health-related questions and receive responses grounded in clinical research. Answers are supported by peer-reviewed medical sources, including publications such as The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA and Nature, according to Apple and OpenEvidence. Users can rate responses and provide feedback on factors such as relevance, detail and usefulness. Participants will also be asked to complete regular surveys to help researchers better understand how AI-generated health information is interpreted and used.Apple targets up to 200,000 participantsApple is planning to enrol around 2,00,000 adults in the United States for the virtual study. The eligible participants must be at least 21 years old and use an iPhone 15-series device or later running iOS 26 or above. The participants can optionally share the HealthKit data information such as activity, sleep, heart rate and lab results enabling the app to create more personalised responses. The tech giant said that the data will be anonymised before being sent to a secure third-party cloud provider and will not be used to train AI models. OpenEvidence will delete query and response data after 24 hours, according to the company.Privacy and safeguardsApple says the study was designed with privacy protections, transparency and clinical guardrails. Study data won’t be used to train AI models, and participants control whether to share HealthKit metrics or survey responses. The app has safety guardrails meant to detect certain concerning questions and suggest following up with a provider or other resources. Apple stresses that the app isn’t meant to diagnose or treat any condition or replace a medical professional’s advice.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: So what does a severe AQI day actually mean for a Delhi family’s daily routine?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: By the afternoon of 14 November Delhi’s overall AQI was 363, officially very poor.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: By the afternoon of 14 November Delhi’s overall AQI was 363, officially very poor. North Campus, however, recorded 439, Narela 435 and ITO and IIT Delhi 433 each, all falling in the severe zone.That zone starts at 401 the next day, IIT Delhi was at 425, while the city average settled at 352. Which side of that line your neighbourhood sits on shapes your whole day.The day begins with a numberTake for instance a family in Punjabi Bagh where the reading touched 406 on 14 November. The windows are shut and the morning walk is canceled. Commuters are advised to wear a well-fitting N95 outdoors.Under GRAP stage II, parking fees are hiked to discourage use of private cars while Metro and bus frequency is increased. Even the trip to and from is a calculation.School is a negotiationAfter the commission for air quality management imposed GRAP stage III on November 6, Delhi schools moved to hybrid classes up to Class 5 from November 7.It sounds like flexibility but it actually means deciding whether to send a six-year-old out into the smog or find someone to supervise at home. It is this choice that bites hardest for households where both adults work outside.The waiting room in the clinicOn November 9, some 50 patients with breathing difficulty came to the respiratory OPD at a south Delhi hospital. Its estimated that a up to 75 per cent rise in such cases during times of severe pollution.Doctors say there is an expected increase of 20-30 per cent in respiratory OPD and emergency visits and those in the age group of 20-50 are also complaining of breathing trouble. So a cough means inhalers, a doctor’s visit and often a day off work.Why does it keep repeating itselfFireworks get the blame but the baseline was already bad. CSE found that Delhi’s average PM2.5 in the week before Diwali was 236 µg/m³, a three-year high. This is 97 per cent higher than 2025’s 120 and 32 per cent higher than 2024’s 179.On Diwali day itself, CREA estimates the daily average at 257 µg/m³, the fourth most polluted Diwali since 2016. India’s 24-hour PM2.5 standard is 60.And pollution from neighboring NCR districts accounted for around 54 per cent of Delhi’s PM2.5 in the first eight days of November, so a household can do everything right and still breathe it in.Seasonal taxThe numbers also swing quickly. The city counted 352 on Sunday morning and 290 by 4pm That’s the real cost of whiplash. Families don't plan for an average, they plan for the worst reading.Those with purifiers and flexible jobs adapt; those without just take it on the chin.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: An Illinois World War II veteran who fought in Europe at 18 and helped liberate Dachau has received France’s Legion of Honor at 102; he still lives independently and drives, more than eight decades after the war
articles.summary: A 102-year-old World War II veteran from Illinois, who fought in Europe at the age of 18 and helped liberate the Dachau concentration camp in Germany, has
articles.body: A 102-year-old World War II veteran from Illinois, who fought in Europe at the age of 18 and helped liberate the Dachau concentration camp in Germany, has received France’s prestigious Legion of Honor. William Lyford, a resident of Woodstock, was presented with the distinction on November 13 in recognition of his service during the war. According to ABC7 Chicago, which reported the ceremony, Lyford continues to live independently in his home and still drives, more than eight decades after returning from the battlefield.The ceremony brought together Lyford's family, friends and fellow veterans to recognise his contribution to the Allied efforts during World War II. The French government awarded him the Legion of Honor, France's highest national distinction, in recognition of his role in helping liberate the country from Nazi occupation. The honour also acknowledges the sacrifices made by American servicemen who fought alongside French forces and their allies during the conflict.Lyford was just 18 when he served in Europe in 1945. His wartime service included time in France towards the end of the conflict, as well as participation in the liberation of Dachau, one of Nazi Germany's most notorious concentration camps, located near Munich. His military record already includes several American decorations, including the Bronze Star and the Combat Infantry Badge.The liberation of Dachau remains one of the defining moments of the final months of World War II. Established by the Nazi regime in March 1933, Dachau was the first regular concentration camp and became a model for the wider network of camps that followed. It held political prisoners, Jewish people and others persecuted by the Nazis, with inmates subjected to forced labour, starvation, disease and systematic brutality.According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, American forces liberated Dachau on April 29, 1945. Soldiers from the 42nd and 45th Infantry Divisions and the 20th Armored Division took part in the operation, freeing approximately 32,000 prisoners. As they approached the camp, American troops encountered overwhelming evidence of Nazi atrocities, including railway cars filled with the bodies of prisoners who had died during transportation.The liberation came as Allied forces advanced deeper into Germany and the Nazi regime approached defeat. For survivors who had endured years of imprisonment, the arrival of American soldiers marked the end of captivity, although many were left severely weakened by hunger, disease and abuse.For Lyford, the experience was part of his service as an infantryman during the final phase of the war in Europe. He left the military in 1945 and returned to civilian life in the United States. He subsequently built a career in construction contracting, moving away from the battlefields and towards a profession that would occupy much of his post-war life.More than 80 years later, his daughter April Kopplin travelled from Colorado to attend the ceremony in Woodstock. She recalled that her father rarely spoke about his wartime experiences while she was growing up. His military past was not something the family regularly discussed, and she occasionally came across photographs from that period instead."Once in a while. I'd see a picture in a box in the house somewhere. That was it. They just didn't make a big deal out of it. They came home and made a life for themselves," Kopplin told ABC7 Chicago.Despite his age, Lyford continues to maintain an independent lifestyle. He remains in his Woodstock home and still drives, a detail that has drawn attention alongside the recognition of his wartime service. His longevity also made the occasion particularly significant for the local veterans' community.John Widmayer, a Vietnam veteran, expressed pride in Lyford's achievement and his continued presence among the community's surviving veterans. "Our VFW is very proud of him. There aren't many post that can say they have a 102 year old veteran infantryman still alive," Widmayer said.French Consul General Charlotte Mantel also attended the event and spoke about the significance of recognising veterans who helped secure France's freedom during the war. She said Lyford's contribution reflected the enduring alliance between the two countries. "What Mr Lyford did during the second world war was showcasing what this alliance means. We are so grateful for what he did," Mantel said.The Legion of Honor was established on May 19, 1802, by Napoleon Bonaparte and remains France's highest national decoration. According to the French institution responsible for administering the order, it recognises individuals for outstanding merit and contributions to the public good. While it is awarded to both military personnel and civilians, it has also been used to recognise foreign veterans who played a role in France's liberation during World War II.For Lyford, the recognition was something he had never expected to receive. Reflecting on the honour, he told ABC7 Chicago: "This is truly an honor that I never dreamt of." He also revealed that he planned to place the medal on his pillow when he went to sleep that night, marking a personal moment after a lifetime that had taken him from the battlefields of Europe to a quiet home in Illinois.You use AI every day. articles.title: When mathematics turns into physics: Newton’s law of universal gravitation
articles.summary: Sir Isaac Newton is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in the history of science.
articles.body: Sir Isaac Newton is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in the history of science. He was a polymath with contributions extended across mathematics, physics, astronomy, Alchemy, optics, theology, and public administration. Among his most significant achievements were the development of calculus, the formulation of the laws of motion and universal gravitation, the explanation of celestial mechanics, and advances in optical science including the invention of the reflecting telescope.Newton’s work transformed humanity’s understanding of the natural world and established many of the foundations of classical physics and modern science. By combining observation and mathematical formulae with physical reasoning, he helped create a scientific-framework through which natural phenomena could be described, explained, and predicted with remarkable precision. His contemporary, Alexander Pope, captured the impact of Newton’s achievements in the famous lines:“Nature and Nature’s laws lay hid in night;God said, Let Newton be! and all was light.”Few scientific contributions have had a more profound influence on our understanding of the physical universe than the “Law of Universal Gravitation.” Popular tradition attributes its origin to the famous story of a falling apple, which is an example of the famous "Aha!" or "Eureka!" moments associated with so many scientific discoveries and retold countless times. While the historical accuracy of this anecdote remains uncertain, the story illustrates an important aspect of scientific discovery: the ability to transform ordinary observations into universal principles.The concept of gravitation, however, did not begin with Newton. For centuries, philosophers and scholars sought to explain why objects fall and why celestial bodies move across the heavens. Aristotle’s idea of gravity was the natural tendency of objects to move toward its proper place, i.e., center of the universe. While lighter substances like air or smoke exhibit an opposing tendency of buoyancy or levity. This was the most influential framework of the ancient world, according to which a stone falls because it seeks the center of the Earth (which Aristotle considered as center of the universe).Important advances also emerged in other intellectual traditions. Indian scholars came up with more accurate idea. Brahmagupta described the Earth as possessing an attractive force that draws objects toward it, while later writers, including Bhaskara II, discussed forces responsible for objects to fall toward the Earth. Islamic scholars also, like Al-Biruni and others, made significant contributions to the study of planetary motion and critically examined aspects of Aristotelian physics.Most early explanations were qualitative and speculative, lacking the mathematical structure necessary for precise prediction. During the Scientific Revolution, thinkers started questioning Aristotelian physics. Galileo demonstrated experimentally that objects of different masses fall at nearly the same rate in the absence of air resistance, overturning a key Aristotelian belief that heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects. Johannes Kepler described the mathematical laws of planetary motion. Despite these advances, no one had yet established a universal physical-mathematical framework connecting terrestrial and celestial phenomena. The transition from philosophical speculation to quantitative science marks one of the defining features of modern physics, and Newton played a central role in that transformation.Newton’s achievement was to unify these diverse strands of knowledge into a single quantitative theory. By uniting mathematics and physics, he demonstrated that natural phenomena could be explained through universal physical laws expressed in mathematical form. He proposed that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass through a force governed by a precise mathematical relationship. This insight united the motion of falling objects on Earth with the movement of planets and moons in the heavens.The “Law of Universal Gravitation” is expressed as:where F is the gravitational force between two objects, G is the universal gravitational constant, m₁ and m₂ are their masses, and r is the distance between their centers. In most simple terms, the law states that gravitational attraction increases with mass and decreases with the distance between objects. Most importantly, it applies universally, from falling apples to orbiting planets.Newton’s greatest contribution was not merely the discovery of a law of gravitation but the demonstration that nature operates according to universal principles. Till the 16th century, astronomy had evolved as a mathematical discipline with an observational component. Kepler’s challenge of finding the true, physical orbits of the planets and their causes (why planets move so) were recognized as the chief goal of planetary theory. Newton’s accomplishment was the completion of Kepler’s quest to turn astronomy into physics. Newton transformed astronomy from a discipline concerned primarily with describing celestial motions mathematically, into a true physical science of explaining them.This achievement required a profound change in worldview. Although the cosmos was transformed from geo-centric to helio-centric before Newton; the heavens and the earth were still believed to be fundamentally different realms governed by distinct principles. Aristotle believed that the motion in the heavens was fundamentally different from motion on the earth. Because of developments in philosophy and theology in the 17th century, especially the trend toward banishing minds and souls from the physical universe, the heavens came to be seen as not radically distinct from the earth. Thousands of years before, the Indian mind has reached similar conclusions (Yajurveda: Yatha pinde tatha brahmande). However, this Indian idea of equating the microcosm with the macrocosm or the human body with the cosmic body remained more philosophical than scientific and it took the distinct form of a scientific idea in the hands of Newton.Newton rejected this separation of the heavens and the earth and in doing so, he recast mathematics as physics. Through the combined power of his laws of motion and universal gravitation, he unified the earthly and celestial mechanics and showed that the same forces and laws govern both terrestrial and celestial phenomena. He established the foundations of classical physics and demonstrated the power of mathematics as the language of nature. It established that the cosmos runs on universal principles which can be reduced to mathematical formulae with immense power of prediction. His universal gravitation and mathematical methods created a new context in which astronomical problems were investigated. The great distance of stars, which had once seemed such an implausible concomitant to the helio-centric planetary arrangement, was now seen as a necessary consequence of universal gravitation, a means of keeping the universe from collapsing on itself. The stars themselves were now seen as independent bodies moving through space.The “Law of Universal Gravitation” has quantitatively explained ocean tides as the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on the Earth's oceans. It serves as the mathematical backbone for calculating trajectories for launching artificial satellites, landing on the moon and space missions. How to apply gravitational theory to explain ever more subtle anomalies in planetary astronomy, became the most important question. Discrepancies in predicted versus observed planetary orbits (such as Uranus) allowed scientists to use Newton’s law to mathematically predict and discover new planets like Neptune. Ultimately, the inability to explain some subtle anomalies in planetary astronomy encouraged scientists to find alternate theories. Although Newton's law is superseded in the 20th century by Albert Einstein’s Theory of General Relativity for extreme conditions (such as massive gravitational fields, high speeds near the speed of light), it is still the primary tool used for everyday physics, engineering, and space navigation within our solar system.B Purushartha is an IAS officer and Asian Development Bank Director’s Adviser, recognised for making Chandigarh the first million-plus ODF city.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.summary: There is nothing deader than dead. As Joseph Heller so successfully puts it in Catch-22, “Clewinger was dead.
articles.body: There is nothing deader than dead. As Joseph Heller so successfully puts it in Catch-22, “Clewinger was dead. That was the flaw in his philosophy?” You cannot nuance your way out of that sentence.The absoluteness of death is something we like to resist. Immortality is among the oldest of human desires. Less ambitiously, but just as significantly, there is the drive towards longevity, so much in evidence today. Tech bros most famously spend enormous time and effort ensuring that their precious beings are preserved for the benefit of the rest of us for as long as possible. Hyperbaric chambers, cold plunging, infrared saunas, red-light therapy and a few dozen supplements every day are all part of the regime.But death is cruelly indifferent to our sense of our own specialness. The atoms that make us up go on, eventually, to become other things. We experience the decay of our bodies as something significant, but in the larger scheme, all that happens is that matter changes shape and form.What exactly do we mean when we say that something is alive? We may be better served by asking not about what living things are but what they do. They take in nourishment from the outside world to keep themselves going and expel what they don't need. They are continually repairing and renewing themselves. Living things resist for a while the tug of disorder, although eventually it’s a losing battle. A living thing is not merely an object but a process. When that process stops, it dies.The idea that living beings are processes rather than things is both obvious and counterintuitive, if such a thing is possible. We are forms; we are made up of substance, as is all life, and to think of ourselves as flows rather than stocks is not easy.Part of the reason is that we need to make no conscious effort to keep the processes of life going. We breathe, our hearts beat, our food gets digested all by itself. We don't carry the burden of continuity. Had we been responsible for these, we would have had time for little else. The unconscious nature of staying alive makes it feel that life is the default state.The shock of seeing a lifeless body comes from the fact that, at one level, the object looks intact. All of what we thought of as ourselves looks like it hits us. The body now no apparent indication of what was about to happen; some vital process just stopped. The shock of people dying before their time reveals our implicit mental model of life.That is because death is absolute in a way decay is not. An object can be damaged bit by bit; we get that. But the process of being alive is different. When it finally stops, there is no restarting it. We can put someone in an induced coma, but that is merely dimming the lights, not extinguishing them. And for those who freeze their bodies and hope for future technology to bring them back to their original selves, so far, that's just a hope. And I am not dying to find out how that works out.The truth is that when the process finally ends, we stop existing. There is no threshold to cross, no ‘other side’. The problem is, even if we are not merely objects, we need to experience ourselves as enduring beings. To experience ourselves as we actually are, an intricate web of processes constantly adjusting to the world around us to keep us alive, would be deeply disorienting. A stable self is what lets us love someone over time and feel responsible for what we do, and for that we have to feel like the same person from one day to the next.A switch has been flipped, and our entire entity has, for all practical purposes, disappeared. That we are patterns made possible by a process calls for us to look beyond the manner in which we experience ourselves.Since death typically happens with age, when we see the gradual signs of the body withering, it seems as if it is a failure of the physical self. Bit by bit, the body becomes decrepit and loses strength till one day it gives up. Decay and deterioration are things we understand. All physical objects degrade with time, and so does our body.It is when a fit young person dies at a gym while working out that the shock hits us. The body now no apparent indication of what was about to happen; some vital process just stopped. The shock of people dying before their time reveals our implicit mental model of life.That is because death is absolute in a way decay is not. An object can be damaged bit by bit; we get that. But the process of being alive is different. When it finally stops, there is no restarting it. We can put someone in an induced coma, but that is merely dimming the lights, not extinguishing them. And for those who freeze their bodies and hope for future technology to bring them back to their original selves, so far, that's just a hope. And I am not dying to find out how that works out.The truth is that when the process finally ends, we stop existing. There is no threshold to cross, no ‘other side’. The problem is, even if we are not merely objects, we need to experience ourselves as enduring beings. To experience ourselves as we actually are, an intricate web of processes constantly adjusting to the world around us to keep us alive, would be deeply disorienting. A stable self is what lets us love someone over time and feel responsible for what we do, and for that we have to feel like the same person from one day to the next.A switch has been flipped, and our entire entity has, for all practical purposes, disappeared. That we are patterns made possible by a process calls for us to look beyond the manner in which we experience ourselves.Another way to think about life is as a flame, and, in fact, life itself can be thought of as an “akhand diya”, a lamp that is never extinguished. A flame lights another, and while individual flames die out, the fire never goes out. Or think of the jamun of dahi, where the living cultures of the curd travel from one bowl to another, from one home to another, one century to another. But the flame that goes out does not come back.To come back to where we started, there is nothing deader than dead. No mysterious substance has been subtracted. The matter that made up the body remains. None of it, by itself, was the life. The river stopped flowing. That's all.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Workers should get paid time off to train for national crises, say peers
articles.summary: A House of Lords committee says more preparation is needed for war, power cuts, and cyber-attacks.
articles.body:
Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended.

In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income.

It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters.

It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies.

In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step".

But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks.

It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters.

The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic.

It noted that the previous government floated the idea of a "civilian reservist cadre" to help out in times of crisis in its 2021 defence review, but this was dropped when the report was updated two years later.

Although some employers offer time off to staff who volunteer, there is currently no legal entitlement to paid leave for those in roles such as coastguard rescue, firefighting, or the St John Ambulance.

Army reservists can claim up to £400 a day from the government to cover lost pay if they are mobilised, but employers do not have to allow time off for training - although some choose to do so.

In their report, the peers said a new right to paid time off could cover "approved" training and volunteering, without specifying exact roles.

They did not recommend an exact leave entitlement, instead suggesting that Labour ministers should work with employers to design "proportionate arrangements" for workers.

Elsewhere in their report, peers recommended the government should send booklets to every household with information about what to do in a crisis, modelled on those sent to homes in Sweden and Denmark.

In its evidence to the inquiry, the government said it planned to provide information through its website - but peers rejected this approach, adding it risked "excluding some groups" and would not work during prolonged periods of disruption.

The peers also recommended the development of a multilingual "public preparedness app" to access official guidance on preparing for emergencies.

It should also allow users to automatically share their location with emergency authorities, similar to the 112 Suomi app in Finland, they added.

The Cabinet Office said it would "carefully review" the report, whilst insisting the government was already taking action to improve crisis resilience.

It pointed to work already under way to update departments' secret defence plans, known as the "war book", and a major exercise scheduled for next year to test the the UK's resilience for war.

The government also recently announced new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables, including powers for officials to inspect cable landing stations owned and operated by telecom companies.
